h1:
Sakon Nakhon–Udon Thani Road Trip
Two Upper-Isan Cities in 3 Days, 2 Nights
intro: Sakon Nakhon and Udon Thani are two Upper-Isan cities sitting on the same road — the Nittayo Road (Highway 22). The two town centres are about 160 kilometres apart, a two-and-a-half to three-hour drive, so it's easy to roll both into one trip. This plan runs 3 days and 2 nights: start in Sakon Nakhon for the city's revered Wat Phra That Choeng Chum, Nong Han lake and the Ban Don Koi indigo-dyeing village, then drive up to Udon to see the Red Lotus Sea at Kumphawapi, stop at the World Heritage site of Ban Chiang, and finish with Kham Chanot — all with rough timings, entry fees, boat prices and eateries that are actually open in 2026 so you can plan it right.

blocks.html: A lot of people fly into Udon and then dither over whether Sakon Nakhon is worth the detour — or they come to Sakon Nakhon and end up wishing they'd seen the Red Lotus Sea. The truth is you don't have to choose. The two provinces are joined by the Nittayo Road, an easy straight drive on mostly flat terrain, and it's only about two and a half hours from one town centre to the other. This plan starts in Sakon Nakhon because the in-town sights are clustered close enough to walk between, then works its way up to Udon, which has more return flights. If you fly into Udon instead, just flip the order of the days — the route is the same.

blocks.text: Why pair Sakon Nakhon with Udon Thani

blocks.html: The main reasons are the short distance and the way the two cities complement each other — you're not seeing the same kind of thing twice. Sakon Nakhon is a city of temples and craft, while Udon is a bigger city with both cool-season nature and Vietnamese food. Here's what each one gives you.

items.name: Sakon Nakhon — temples, craft and Nong Han
items.blurb: The revered Wat Phra That Choeng Chum sits right in the middle of the city, alongside the Ajahn Mun forest-monk museum, Nong Han (Isan's big freshwater lake), and indigo-dyeing villages that ship their cloth as far as Japan. A good way to open the trip with a mix of merit-making and handicraft.

items.name: Udon Thani — red lotus, Ban Chiang and Vietnamese food
items.blurb: In winter the Red Lotus Sea at Kumphawapi blooms across the whole water. There's the World Heritage site of Ban Chiang, Nong Prajak park in the city centre, and Vietnamese food like nam neuang that doubles as the city's signature souvenir. A solid way to close the trip in a bigger city.

items.name: The link — the Nittayo Road
items.blurb: Highway 22 connects the two cities over about 160 km, passing Phang Khon, Sawang Daen Din and Nong Han. The terrain is flat and easy, and the road runs right past Ban Chiang so you can stop before reaching Udon. So this isn't just a transfer between cities — there are sights along the way.

items: Distance — about 160 km from central Sakon Nakhon to central Udon Thani along the Nittayo Road (Highway 22), passing Phang Khon, Sawang Daen Din and Nong Han.
Driving time — usually two and a half to three hours; mostly flat and easy, but expect traffic lights and slow stretches when you pass through the district towns.
Van/bus — vans and buses run all day between the Sakon Nakhon and Udon Thani bus terminals, fares in the low hundreds of THB per trip, taking around 3 hours.
Flights — both cities have airports (Sakon Nakhon SNO and Udon Thani UTH); if you can find tickets to fly into one and out of the other, it saves more time than flying in and out of the same point.
Car rental — the most flexible option, since the Red Lotus Sea, Ban Chiang, Kham Chanot and the indigo villages are all outside the towns and hard to reach by public transport.

blocks.title: Get the direction and timing right
blocks.html: If seeing the Red Lotus Sea is the goal, plan the trip for December to early March, when the lotus blooms thickest, and get to the pier before 11am because the flowers close up later in the morning when the sun gets strong. That's why this plan puts the Red Lotus Sea as the early-morning activity on the Udon day. If you come at another time of year, swap it for Kham Chanot or Wat Pa Phu Kon instead so you don't end up disappointed.

blocks.text: Day 1 — Sakon Nakhon: city temple, Nong Han and indigo cloth

blocks.html: Day one stays entirely on the Sakon Nakhon side. Morning is for Wat Phra That Choeng Chum in the city centre and the Ajahn Mun museum, both within walking distance. In the afternoon head out to Nong Han and the indigo village outside town, then come back into the city for dinner. It's a day that mixes merit-making, handicraft and unhurried lakeside nature.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Sakon Nakhon: Choeng Chum–Nong Han–indigo cloth

items.activity: Pay respects at Wat Phra That Choeng Chum Worawihan in central Sakon Nakhon
items.note: The city's most revered stupa, right in the middle of the province; pay respects to Luang Pho Ong Saen, the temple's twin Buddha image. Free entry. Go early before it fills up. Dress modestly and take off your shoes before stepping onto the platform.

items.activity: Ajahn Mun Bhuridatto Museum at Wat Pa Sutthawat
items.note: In town, a short drive on from the stupa. It displays the story of Luang Pu Mun and his real belongings, with a wax figure and a quiet atmosphere. Free entry.

items.activity: Lunch on Vietnamese food at Willy Nam Neuang
items.note: An old Vietnamese restaurant on Rat Phatthana Road, open daily 10:30–21:30. Try the nam neuang (fresh pork spring rolls), fried mu yo and Phon Yang Kham beef pho. Mains run from tens to the low hundreds of THB.

items.activity: Nong Han, the largest freshwater lake in Isan
items.note: On the southern edge of the city, with a lakeside park and a boat launch out to Don Sawan island. Cool breeze in the afternoon.

items.activity: Drive to Ban Don Koi indigo-dyeing village, Phanna Nikhom district
items.note: About 38 km from the city. Watch indigo dyeing and weaving demonstrations at Witchalai Don Koi or Home Khram Mae Waree. Best to call ahead (087-232-9016). The last stretch is a dirt road.

items.activity: Head back to town for an Isan dinner and overnight in central Sakon Nakhon
items.note: Try Saba-nga in the city centre or Suan Mai Hom on Sukkasem Road — order jaew hon, larb or som tam — or stroll the evening market for grilled snacks.

blocks.title: Call ahead before going to Ban Don Koi
blocks.html: The indigo village is a real working community, not a shop that's open all the time. If you want to see the full dyeing and weaving process, call the weaving group or Home Khram Mae Waree a day ahead (087-232-9016), because on some days the women are busy in the fields. The last 12 km or so into the village is a dirt road that gets slippery in the rain, so drive slowly. If you'd rather not head far out of town, you can swap in an indigo-cloth shop in central Sakon Nakhon instead.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Drive the Nittayo Road up to Udon, stop at Ban Chiang, into the city by evening

blocks.html: Day two is the crossover day. Leave Sakon Nakhon in the morning and drive the Nittayo Road toward Udon, stopping at Ban Chiang to see the World Heritage site right along the way, then reach Udon in the late afternoon. In the evening take in Nong Prajak park and some food in the city. It's a day that delivers both history and big-city atmosphere.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Crossing to Udon: Ban Chiang–Nong Prajak

items.activity: Leave Sakon Nakhon, get on the Nittayo Road (Highway 22) toward Udon
items.note: Fill up the tank. Flat and easy driving, passing Phang Khon, Sawang Daen Din and Nong Han.

items.activity: Ban Chiang National Museum, Nong Han district
items.note: A World Heritage site of prehistoric pottery; see the painted designs and the real excavation pits. Entry 30 THB for Thais. Open Tuesday–Sunday 09:00–16:00, closed Monday.

items.activity: Lunch around Nong Han or carry on into Udon
items.note: If you're hungry before the city, there are Isan and noodle spots along the Nittayo Road near Nong Han, or hold out and eat at a place in central Udon.

items.activity: Arrive in Udon Thani, check in at a hotel in town
items.note: The area around Nong Prajak or near UD Town is convenient — close to food and markets.

items.activity: Nong Prajak park and the giant yellow duck
items.note: A city-centre park where locals come to exercise and take photos, with the giant yellow duck as a landmark. Cool breeze in the evening. Free entry.

items.activity: Dinner at UD Town or the walking street
items.note: UD Town is next to the train station, with restaurants and a beer garden, while the Udon walking street runs Friday–Sunday near Nong Prajak — plenty to eat as you stroll.

blocks.title: Ban Chiang is closed on Mondays
blocks.html: The Ban Chiang museum is closed every Monday. If your day two happens to fall on a Monday, swap in the Wat Pho Si Nai excavation pit inside Ban Chiang village instead (open daily, with real skeletons and pots in the pit), or shift the museum to the following day. The other stops on the route are open every day as usual.

blocks.text: Day 3 — Red Lotus Sea at dawn, last Udon highlights before heading home

blocks.html: The last day starts before dawn, because the Red Lotus Sea looks best during golden hour. Head out to Kumphawapi and take a boat to see the lotus in bloom before the sun gets strong, then come back into the city mid-morning for breakfast. After that, pick between Kham Chanot and Wat Pa Phu Kon depending on your time, buy some souvenirs and head home. It's a day that closes the trip with cool-season nature you can only catch at this time of year.

items.activity: Leave the city for the Red Lotus Sea, Kumphawapi district
items.note: About 40 km from Udon, roughly a 50-minute drive. You need to set out before dawn to catch the lotus in bloom before the sun gets strong (only possible in winter, December to early March).

items.activity: Boat trip on the Red Lotus Sea, Nong Han Kumphawapi
items.note: Board at Ban Diam or Ban Chiang Haeo pier. A small 2-seat boat is about 300 THB, a large 6-seat boat about 500 THB. Piers open 06:00–17:00; 6–11am is the prettiest window.

items.activity: Back into Udon for breakfast or coffee
items.note: Find a café or breakfast spot in town; there are plenty of cafés around Nong Prajak and the city centre.

items.activity: Kham Chanot or Wat Pa Phu Kon (pick based on time and interest)
items.note: Kham Chanot is a sacred forest in the middle of water, in Ban Dung district, open 06:00–18:00, while Wat Pa Phu Kon has a white marble reclining Buddha, open 08:30–17:00. They're in different directions, so choose just one if you have an afternoon flight.

items.activity: Buy souvenirs, then head to the airport/bus terminal in Udon
items.note: The most popular souvenirs are nam neuang and mu yo. Stop at VT Nam Neuang on Mittraphap Road (open 09:00–20:00) to buy some to take home. Udon airport is close to the city — allow extra time for afternoon traffic.

blocks.title: On the season and timing your days
blocks.html: The Red Lotus Sea is a highlight you can only visit in winter, roughly December to early March. At other times of year the water at Nong Han Kumphawapi has no lotus flowers to see, so check first whether you're hitting the right season. If you're not, cut it and go all-in on both Kham Chanot and Wat Pa Phu Kon instead, so you don't end up rising at dawn only to find an empty lake.

blocks.text: Food in both cities worth trying

blocks.html: The Sakon Nakhon–Udon route gives you two food traditions to try. Both cities have had Thai-Vietnamese communities for a long time, so Vietnamese food is strong in each, while the Isan side has jaew hon and Phon Yang Kham beef pho as local standouts. Here are spots that are actually open in 2026 and that locals go to, ordered by how well they fit this trip's route.

items.name: Willy Nam Neuang (Sakon Nakhon)
items.blurb: An old Vietnamese restaurant in Sakon Nakhon — soft-skinned nam neuang, a rich dipping sauce, big slices of fried mu yo, and Phon Yang Kham beef pho so good it needs no seasoning. This is where locals bring guests to eat and buy souvenirs; it's also sold at Sakon Nakhon airport.
items.meta: Rat Phatthana Rd, Sakon Nakhon city · open daily 10:30–21:30

items.name: VT Nam Neuang (Udon Thani)
items.blurb: The original nam neuang of Udon, with a branch at Ban Chan Yai and a drive-through. It does both dine-in and Vietnamese-style souvenirs — nam neuang, mu yo, pak mo yuan. A spot Udon locals have long recommended for picking up souvenirs before heading home.
items.meta: Mittraphap Rd, Ban Chan branch · open daily 09:00–20:00

items.name: Saba-nga (Sakon Nakhon)
items.blurb: A traditional Isan restaurant in central Sakon Nakhon with comfortable air-conditioned seating and parking — good for a family dinner after a full day out. Order larb, koi, som tam and a full range of local dishes.
items.meta: Central Sakon Nakhon · comfortable air-conditioned seating

items.name: Suan Mai Hom Isan food (Sakon Nakhon)
items.blurb: An affordable Isan spot on Sukkasem Road, known for jaew hon with pla khang, deep-fried tilapia salad and fried pork larb. Opens early, good for a first meal of the day or a quick lunch.
items.meta: Sukkasem Rd, That Choeng Chum, Sakon Nakhon city · opens early 06:00–13:00

items.name: Jaew Hon UD Town (Udon Thani)
items.blurb: Isan-style dinner — a herbal-broth hot pot for dipping fresh pork. The UD Town area has several places to choose from and a lively atmosphere in the evening. A good way to close the Udon day with a filling, affordable meal.
items.meta: UD Town area, next to Udon train station · open evening to late

items.name: Phon Yang Kham beef pho
items.blurb: Phon Yang Kham is Sakon Nakhon's famous fattened beef, turned into pho with a clear, bone-sweet broth or grilled with jaew dipping sauce. You'll find it at both Vietnamese and beef restaurants in Sakon Nakhon city — a flavour that tells you you've truly reached the region.
items.meta: Found in Sakon Nakhon city · Vietnamese and beef restaurants

items.name: Evening market / walking street, Sakon Nakhon
items.blurb: Grilled and fried snacks, local sweets and roadside Isan food in Sakon Nakhon city. Good for grazing on the first evening without sitting down at a restaurant — easy on the wallet, and you can try several things in one meal.
items.meta: Sakon Nakhon city · evening to night

items.name: Udon walking street (Nong Prajak)
items.blurb: Open Friday–Sunday near Nong Prajak park, a long stretch of both savoury and sweet — Vietnamese, Isan and snacks. Good if your trip falls on a weekend, with the feel of Udon by night.
items.meta: Beside Nong Prajak, Udon Thani · Fri–Sun, evening to night

blocks.text: Add-ons if you have more than 3 days

blocks.html: If you stretch the trip to 4 days or want a more relaxed pace, there are several more temple and nature spots along the route you can add based on your interests.

items: Wat Tham Pha Daen, Sakon Nakhon — cliff carvings and a Naga figure on the Phu Phan range, with a viewpoint over Sakon Nakhon city. The final climb is steep, so take the curves carefully. Good to slot into day one if you start early.

Kham Chanot and Wat Pa Phu Kon — if you don't have an early flight home on the last day, you can fit both. Kham Chanot is a sacred forest in the middle of water, while Wat Pa Phu Kon has a white marble reclining Buddha set in the forest.
Udon Thani City Museum — the old Rachinuthit building in central Udon, telling the city's history and its wartime era. Good for a rainy day or a break from the sun, and easy to reach in town.

Indigo cloth and Sakon Nakhon souvenirs — beyond Ban Don Koi, there are hand-dyed indigo shops in the city to pick up as a local-only souvenir. The patterns and indigo shades differ from one community to the next.
Car rental — an eco-car or sedan runs about 900–1,400 THB/day, not including fuel; split among a few people it's the best value for this trip.
Intercity van/bus — Sakon Nakhon–Udon is in the low hundreds of THB per trip, but you'll still need onward transport in town.
Accommodation — guesthouses start in the low hundreds, mid-range hotels around 700–1,800 THB/night; both Sakon Nakhon and Udon have plenty to choose from.

Entry/boat fees — Ban Chiang 30 THB for Thais; Wat Phra That Choeng Chum and the Ajahn Mun museum are free; a Red Lotus Sea boat is 300 THB for a small boat, 500 THB for a large boat (which you can split).
Check the Red Lotus Sea season — only possible roughly December to early March; outside that there are no lotus flowers, so lock in the right window if seeing them is the goal.
Call the indigo village ahead — book Ban Don Koi a day in advance (087-232-9016) so someone is there to demonstrate, and drive the dirt road at the end slowly.
Allow for Ban Chiang's closing day — the Ban Chiang museum is closed Mondays; if your trip falls on a Monday, swap the order or see the Wat Pho Si Nai excavation pit instead.
Carry cash and offerings — flowers, incense and candles are available outside the temples, but some community shops and piers still don't take transfers, so keep cash and drinking water in the car.
Dress modestly at temples — at both Wat Phra That Choeng Chum and Wat Pa Phu Kon, no tank tops or shorts above the knee, and take off your shoes before stepping onto the stupa platform.

faq.q: How many hours is the drive from Sakon Nakhon to Udon Thani?
faq.a: Along the Nittayo Road (Highway 22) it's about 160 kilometres from one town centre to the other, usually two and a half to three hours. The road is mostly flat and easy, but expect traffic lights and slow stretches passing through the district towns. Allow extra time to stop at Ban Chiang along the way too.

faq.q: Can you visit both provinces without a private car?
faq.a: Yes. Vans and buses run all day between the Sakon Nakhon and Udon Thani bus terminals, with fares in the low hundreds of THB. But sights like the Red Lotus Sea, Ban Chiang, Kham Chanot and the indigo villages are outside the towns and awkward by public transport, so if you don't rent a car you should charter a local vehicle or join a tour for those legs.

faq.q: When can you visit the Red Lotus Sea and how much is the boat?
faq.a: The lotus blooms thickest from December to early March. Get to the pier before 11am because the flowers close up later in the morning when the sun gets strong. You can board at Ban Diam or Ban Chiang Haeo pier; a small 2-seat boat is about 300 THB and a large 6-seat boat about 500 THB. The piers are open 06:00–17:00.

faq.q: Should you start in Sakon Nakhon or Udon first?
faq.a: Adjust it to your flights. This plan starts in Sakon Nakhon and finishes in Udon, because Udon has more return flights and the Red Lotus Sea works well as a last-morning activity. If you fly into Udon first, just flip the order of the days — the Nittayo Road route is the same.

faq.q: What do you need to prepare to see indigo cloth at Ban Don Koi?
faq.a: Ban Don Koi is in Phanna Nikhom district, about 38 km from central Sakon Nakhon, and it's a real working community. Call the weaving group or Home Khram Mae Waree a day ahead (087-232-9016) so someone is there to demonstrate the dyeing and weaving. The last 12 km or so into the village is a dirt road that gets slippery in the rain, so drive slowly, and bring cash for buying cloth since some households still don't take transfers.
